chunks: The implication of the language is this: do you not see that when a speaker says, “You only have with me one dirham,” and, “I only ate one loaf,” this indicates the negation of more than one dirham and of eating more than one loaf? It also indicates that the term innamā is assigned for what we have mentioned: Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah have mercy on him, used to hold the permissibility of selling one dirham for two dirhams in a cash transaction, and leading Companions debated him on that and argued against him by the Prophet’s prohibition, peace be upon him and his family, of selling gold for gold and silver for silver, but he opposed them.

ai.seo_question: What does the Arabic term إِنَّمَا imply in legal and hadith interpretation?
ai.summary: This passage explains the linguistic force of the particle إِنَّمَا as indicating restriction and exclusivity. It uses examples from ordinary speech and a legal dispute about exchange transactions to show that the wording limits the meaning to what is explicitly stated. The discussion is relevant to jurisprudence, especially in understanding hadith language and deriving legal rulings.
